title: Assertion-based runtime monitors
description: The oldest invariant monitor: assert statements sprinkled at critical points, checking preconditions, postconditions, and data-structure integrity while the program runs. Cheap, precise, and honest — a violated assertion fails fast at the exact spot the invariant broke instead of corrupting state silently for hours.
method: Insert asserts for key invariants; run with assertions enabled in test/staging; sample in production; log violations with stack context.
usage: Assert invariants, not just input validation; keep production asserts sampled to bound overhead.

demo.code:
balance = 100
balance -= 30
assert balance >= 0, 'invariant violated: negative balance'
print('invariant holds: balance =', balance)

title: Statistical invariant monitors
description: Some invariants are statistical — 'p99 latency under 200ms', 'error rate below 0.1%'. Statistical monitors track distributions over sliding windows and alert when the invariant breaks with significance, distinguishing real drift from noise.
method: Define the metric and window; compute the statistic continuously; alert when it crosses the threshold with significance (not on single samples).
usage: Set thresholds from baselines; require significance before paging; tune windows to the metric's natural timescale.

demo.code:
lat = [120, 130, 125, 400, 128]  # ms
p99 = sorted(lat)[int(0.99 * len(lat))]
print(f'p99 latency {p99}ms:', 'INVARIANT VIOLATED' if p99 > 200 else 'holds')

title: Self-healing invariant restoration
description: Detection is half the job: self-healing monitors restore broken invariants automatically — rebuild a corrupted cache from source, restart a wedged worker, re-queue a lost message. The monitor pairs every watched invariant with a restoration procedure, closing the loop from detection to recovery.
method: For each monitored invariant, define the restore procedure; on violation, attempt restore; escalate to humans only if restore fails.
usage: Test restore procedures like code (they're the real reliability); alert on every auto-restore so humans stay informed.

title: Temporal property runtime monitors
description: Runtime verification monitors check temporal properties on live event streams: 'every request is eventually acknowledged', 'no grant without request'. Tools like JavaMOP and RV-Monitor synthesize monitors from temporal specs and run them alongside production with low overhead.
method: Specify the property (LTL/finite-trace); synthesize the monitor; feed it the event stream; violations trigger handlers.
usage: Monitor the properties tests can't cover (rare interleavings); keep monitor overhead measured.

demo.code:
events = ['request', 'grant', 'request']  # second request ungranted
print('monitor: G(request -> F grant)')
print('stream:', events, '-> VIOLATION: request without grant')

title: Invariant mining from logs
description: Production logs contain implicit invariants: 'every charge is followed by a receipt within 5s'. Mining logs for frequent temporal patterns surfaces the system's actual contracts — often surprising the team — which then become monitors. The logs teach you what to watch.
method: Mine frequent patterns from logs (sequence mining); present candidates to engineers; promote confirmed ones to monitors.
usage: Mine periodically; have engineers vet candidates (correlation isn't contract); promote the real ones.

demo.code:
logs = ['charge', 'receipt', 'charge', 'receipt']
print('mined pattern: charge -> receipt within 5s (support 100%)')
print('promoted to monitor')

title: Graduated monitor strictness
description: Monitors run at different strictness per environment: pedantic in dev (every invariant checked, failures are errors), sampled in staging, and lightweight in production (only critical invariants, violations alert). Graduated strictness gets thorough checking where it's cheap and safety where it counts.
method: Tag invariants by criticality; configure strictness per environment; dev fails fast, production alerts.

specification.levels: dev pedantic / staging sampled / prod critical
specification.rule: cheap where cheap, safe where counts

usage: Tag every invariant's criticality at authoring time; review the production set quarterly.

title: Data-structure integrity checkers
description: Complex structures (trees, graphs, caches) get periodic integrity walks: a background thread verifies BST ordering, hash-table load factors, or cache coherence invariants. These monitors catch memory corruption and logic bugs that tests miss because they check the live structure, not a test fixture.
method: Write a check_structure() routine; run it periodically or on demand; log and alert on violations with a structure dump.
usage: Run integrity checks in staging always, in production sampled; make the dump actionable.

demo.code:
tree = [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7]  # heap-ordered list
ok = all(tree[i] <= tree[2*i+1] and tree[i] <= tree[2*i+2] for i in range(3))
print('heap invariant:', 'HOLDS' if ok else 'VIOLATED')

title: Watchdog and heartbeat monitors
description: Liveness invariants — 'the worker checks in every 30 seconds' — are monitored by watchdogs: miss N heartbeats and the monitor declares the component dead and triggers recovery. Every robust distributed system has them; they're the simplest invariant monitor that matters.
method: Components emit heartbeats; the watchdog tracks last-seen times; expiry triggers alerts or automatic restart/failover.
usage: Set timeouts from measured heartbeat jitter; make recovery automatic for stateless components.

demo.code:
import time
last_beat = time.time() - 45  # seconds ago
print('last heartbeat 45s ago (timeout 30s) -> WATCHDOG: declare dead, failover')
